gap: No result ChatGPT got states that all three under-$20 contenders stop their PPS at 11 V, and that only one of them claims the 60W-capable AVS that Apple requires for iPhone 18 Pro's top charging speed. The three are the Anker Nano 30W A2147 (PPS 11 V/3 A and 3.3–16 V/2 A per Anker), the Anker Nano Charger Neo A120M (PPS 5–11 V per a USB Connection Information test) and the UGREEN Nexode Air 45W (PPS 5–11 V/4.5 A per Smartzone). None of them offers the 20 V PPS that Pixel 9/10 Pro XL needs. The one with the AVS claim is the A120M Neo, per Anker, at the same $15.99 on anker.com as the Nano 30W that ChatGPT picked.
standout_why: I compared against TechGearLab's Anker Nano 30W review (cited), Android Authority's best USB-C chargers (cited) and Tom's Hardware's best USB chargers (cited; its article body did not render, so only its title was compared). TechGearLab says the Nano 30W is 'not the best charger for the iPhone 18 Pro' but names no under-$20 charger that meets Apple's AVS requirement. Android Authority says the Nano 3 'can't produce the 20V needed by some PPS smartphones' (Pixel 9 Pro XL), but it does not cover the Anker Nano Charger Neo or the UGREEN Nexode Air 45W. Nor does it mention AVS or the Galaxy S26 Ultra's 60 W PPS requirement. So rivals have the Nano 30W half of the finding. No rival maps the under-$20 chargers to Apple's AVS line.
decides: For iPhone 18 Pro owners it changes the pick. Apple's support page lists only the 40W Dynamic adapter or a third-party 60W-capable AVS adapter for the 15-minute tier. The Nano 30W (30 W, no AVS listed by Anker) and the Nexode Air 45W (45 W is below Apple's 60 W line) cannot qualify. The Anker Nano Charger Neo A120M is the only under-$20 charger that claims it, and it costs the same $15.99 on anker.com. That AVS rests on Anker's documents. USB Connection Information did not see AVS profiles from a MacBook Air M5 running PD 3.0, so the page should call it Anker's claim. For Galaxy S26 Ultra (60 W PPS, 5 A cable per SamMobile) and Pixel 9/10 Pro XL (20–21 V PPS per Smartzone), no under-$20 candidate gives top speed. The page should say so rather than name a winner. None of Dealectric's linked USB-C chargers is under $20 (the Nexode Air 65W is $24.99), so the lead writer may need to apply the skip rule.

findings.label: iPhone 18 Pro / Pro Max top-speed wired requirement
findings.value: Apple 40W Dynamic Power Adapter with 60W Max, or a comparable third-party 60W-capable (or greater) adapter that uses Adjustable Voltage Supply (AVS) and supports USB-PD 3.2; about 50% in about 15 minutes
findings.source_title: Fast charge your iPhone - Apple Support
findings.note: Footnote (July 2026 testing): 'USB PD 3.1 (or better) power adapters with Adjustable Voltage Supply (AVS)' with a 60W-capable USB-C cable.

findings.label: iPhone 17 / 17 Pro / 17 Pro Max and iPhone Air fast-charge requirement
findings.value: iPhone 17 series: 40 W adapter or higher for about 50% in about 20 minutes; iPhone 17e and iPhone Air: 20 W or higher for about 50% in about 30 minutes
findings.source_title: Fast charge your iPhone - Apple Support
findings.note: Apple does not mention AVS for the iPhone 17 models, so any 40 W+ USB-PD charger meets Apple's stated line for them.

findings.label: Galaxy S26 Ultra 60 W requirement
findings.value: At least 60 W from one port, USB PD 3.0 or 3.1 with PPS, plus a 5 A USB-C cable (a 3 A cable may work with some PPS chargers)
findings.source_title: Here's what you need to charge Galaxy S26 Ultra at 60W (SamMobile, Abid Iqbal Shaik)
findings.note: SamMobile gives no PPS voltage. The cluster rules cite Android Authority's S26 Ultra test for PPS at 20 V/3 A. I did not open that test.

findings.label: Output profiles (maker)
findings.value: USB-C 5V 3A / 9V 3A / 15V 2A / 20V 1.5A (30 W max); PPS 11V 3A max and 3.3–16V 2A max
findings.note: The page has no AVS and no PPS profile above 16 V. It makes no Samsung or Pixel compatibility statement.

findings.label: Advertised profiles (independent read)
findings.value: 5V 3A, 9V 3A, 15V 3A, 20V 3.25A (65 W) on a 5 A cable / 20V 3A (60 W) on a 3 A cable; PPS 5–11V up to 5 A (5 A cable) or 3 A (3 A cable); box label AVS 9–15V 4.3A, 15–20V 3.25A
findings.source_title: Anker Nano Charger Neo Tested - 65 W at Once, a Xiaomi ID, and No AVS for the Mac (Connection Info, Daniel Gauthier)
findings.note: Read from macOS on a MacBook Air M5, which negotiated USB PD 3.0. AVS PDOs did not appear on the Mac. The site tested no phone, so the iPhone AVS claim stays Anker's. Its PPS tops out at 11 V, with no 20 V PPS. Measured 59.8 W on the 5 A cable and 55.2 W on the 3 A cable.

findings.label: Samsung exclusion (maker)
findings.value: Anker FAQ 'Why does the charger charge Samsung devices at under 45W?': actual power depends on the device; 'Samsung devices may reduce charging power as the battery level increases'
findings.source_title: Why does the charger charge Samsung devices at under 45W? (A120M) - Anker Support
findings.note: Anker's own support page acknowledges that Samsung phones charge below 45 W on this charger.

findings.label: 65 W derating (maker)
findings.value: Gradually reduces power after about 20 minutes at 65 W in normal use
findings.source_title: How is A120M 65W Power Derating Duration? - Anker Support
findings.note: Anker calls this normal thermal protection; timing varies with ambient temperature and the device.

findings.label: Output profiles and phone limits (named reviewer)
findings.value: 5V 3A, 9V 3A, 12V 3A, 15V 3A, 20V 2.25A; PPS 5–11V at 4.5A; Pixel 9/10 Pro XL charge at only about 27 W because they need PPS up to 21 V
findings.note: The reviewer expects current Samsung PPS phones to charge at about 40–45 W (a reviewer estimate; Samsung models not tested) and says both Nexode Air models support SPR AVS. A 45 W maximum is below Apple's '60W-capable' AVS line, so it cannot give iPhone 18 Pro the 15-minute tier. The review links Amazon ASIN B0G6CZ9MFT for the 45W.
